clinicalPearls: Caused by larvae of the raccoon roundworm Baylisascaris procyonis, acquired by ingesting eggs from soil or objects contaminated with raccoon faeces, especially by young children with pica
Human infection produces larva migrans, with a striking tendency for larvae to invade the central nervous system and eyes
Neural larva migrans causes a devastating eosinophilic meningoencephalitis with rapidly progressive encephalopathy, seizures and coma, particularly in toddlers
Ocular larva migrans causes visual loss, and a migrating larva may occasionally be seen in the retina
Marked peripheral and cerebrospinal fluid eosinophilia supports the diagnosis, with serology used for confirmation
Treatment is albendazole together with corticosteroids to limit the inflammatory response, but established neural disease often leaves severe deficits
Prevention centres on avoiding contact with raccoon latrines, cleaning contaminated sites and supervising young children in endemic areas
reference.pathophysiology: Baylisascaris procyonis is an ascarid roundworm whose adults live in the intestine of raccoons, which shed vast numbers of environmentally hardy eggs. Humans are accidental hosts who ingest embryonated eggs from contaminated soil, hands or objects. Larvae hatch in the intestine and, rather than maturing, migrate aggressively through the tissues (visceral, ocular and neural larva migrans). The larvae continue to grow as they migrate and show a marked neurotropism, penetrating the central nervous system where they cause mechanical destruction of neural tissue and provoke an intense eosinophilic inflammatory reaction, producing a fulminant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis. In the eye they damage the retina and incite inflammation. The severity reflects both the larvae's large size and continued growth and the vigorous host immune response along their migratory tracks.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of eosinophilic meningitis such as Angiostrongylus cantonensis
Neurocysticercosis and other cerebral helminthic infection
Toxocara canis neural or ocular larva migrans
Ocular toxocariasis or retinoblastoma (for the eye lesion)
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis or other inflammatory encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count showing marked eosinophilia
Cerebrospinal fluid examination for eosinophilic pleocytosis
MRI of the brain showing periventricular and deep white-matter changes
Serology on serum and cerebrospinal fluid for Baylisascaris
Dilated ophthalmological examination for a migrating retinal larva
Detailed environmental history of raccoon exposure and pica
redFlags: Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or coma in a young child with eosinophilia
New seizures with cerebrospinal fluid eosinophilia
Acute visual loss suggesting ocular larva migrans
Known exposure to a raccoon latrine in a child with neurological symptoms
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is grave once neural larva migrans is established, with a high risk of death or severe permanent neurological disability; early treatment before extensive central nervous system invasion offers the best, though still limited, chance of a good outcome.
pitfalls: Delaying empirical treatment while awaiting confirmatory serology in a rapidly deteriorating child
Overlooking raccoon exposure and pica in the history
Attributing eosinophilic meningitis solely to more familiar causes
Failing to give corticosteroids alongside anthelmintic therapy to temper the inflammatory response
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Start albendazole promptly, ideally pre-emptively after suspected raccoon-roundworm egg ingestion and before central nervous system invasion is established
Give corticosteroids alongside anthelmintic therapy to limit the eosinophilic inflammatory response in neural larva migrans
Provide neurointensive supportive care for seizures, raised intracranial pressure and encephalopathy, with anticonvulsants and ventilatory support as needed
Treat ocular larva migrans with laser photocoagulation of the migrating retinal larva together with corticosteroids
Arrange neurorehabilitation for the frequent residual neurological deficits
Advise environmental control and hygiene measures to remove raccoon latrines and prevent reinfection, particularly in young children with pica
Refer to paediatric infectious diseases, neurology and ophthalmology for multidisciplinary care
